en: The Sutra on Ultimate Great Compassion, Volume Two.
Why is it that the earth element is thus? [Text missing].
What is the fundamental cause of this illness? How is such liberation applied?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
"The great earth of the world bears four kinds of heavy burdens.
The first is the various mountains."
Second, rivers and streams;
third, grasses and trees;
fourth, sentient beings.
Carrying both the pure and the defiled without the mind discriminating between them—
this is called the functional capacity of the earth.
Such is the case with external earth.
The same applies to the internal [body].

The root of illness refers to the failure to dissolve [the pathogenic factors], which results in a discordance with the functions of the earth element. When its function accords with that of the earth element, [it is healthy].
He was immediately freed from his illness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is possible for the earth element to be so."
The fundamental causes of the great disease of water are likewise one hundred and one.
How can it be said that verbal explanation constitutes liberation?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
Your statement that the earth element may be so,
and that the water element and the great elements likewise each have one hundred and one [subdivisions], is not correct.
Why is this? Because worldly water can wash, cleanse, moisten, and soak,
all without making any discrimination.
Because there is no discernment, one does not select what is right from what is wrong.
Because there is no selection of the right from the wrong, defilements and purity alike return to the same source.
Because they return to the same source in true purity, it is called the function of water.
External water is thus;
internal water is likewise.
Because one is cautious regarding water, the true purity merges and flows together, such that defilement and purity are identical in their suchness.
One is immediately liberated from illness.
If one does not exercise caution regarding water and contravenes its natural function—
such that both internally and externally there is discord— this is called the root of illness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it may be so for earth and water;
yet the fire element, the root of great illness, likewise possesses one hundred and one [afflictions]."
"How is it that acting according to what has been taught serves as the function of liberation?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed (Anāvaraṇa), saying:
"The fire of the world burns both the fragrant and the foul."
Just as when there is no discernment, it becomes ash—
uniform in flavor and without distinction—
so too is external fire.
The internal fire is likewise.
When it accords with the fire and causes [the elements] to melt away, this is called the function of liberation;
if it deviates from or opposes it, this is the root of illness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it may be so for earth, water, and fire;
however, the wind disorder, which is the root of all diseases, also has one hundred and one varieties."
"How is it that the World-Honored One speaks of its function as liberation?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed:
"The winds of the world—both fragrant and foul vapors—strike against one another and are universally gathered back into the principle of space."
As it is with external winds,
so it is with internal winds.
To universally gather them in accordance with the wind and return them to the single principle of emptiness is the function of liberation.
"When the functions of wind are contrary and its applications are discordant, this is called the source of illness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if the individual functions of earth, water, fire, and wind are contrary and their fourfold applications are discordant, this is called the source of illness."
What dharma constitutes this?
We only pray that you will, out of compassion and pity for the assembly gathered here and for future sentient beings,
reveal the two dharmas of opposition and compliance so that the multitude may hear them and practice according to the teachings.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:

"The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—are both revered and subject to conditions; when they are in accord, they are non-dual and harmonious, but when they are in conflict, they bring about ten thousand kinds of calamities."
Why is this? Because the earth of the world is conducive to the growth of fruits;
yet to strike it with one's head results in the loss of life, injury to the body, and myriad forms of suffering.
The element of water is likewise;
it conveniently removes impurities and serves people according to their needs.
Yet, if one throws oneself into it, one sinks and drowns as if dead.
The fire element is likewise:
it is conveniently mild and temperate, blowing with moderate force to produce ripening and providing nourishment on a vast scale;
yet, those who cast themselves into it lose their lives.
The wind element is likewise:
when favorable, it stirs, blows, and causes all things to grow;
yet if one casts oneself into the wind, its breath is severed and one is as if dead.
When comparing the internal and external, only that which does not differentiate them accords with the essence of names;
that which opposes them seeks externally.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, although you say that comparing the internal and external makes no distinction between them,
one does not understand the causes for the body's own compliance or resistance."
"I pray that the Buddha, with his vast compassion, will grant me instruction.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
"The physical forms and substances of all sentient beings constitute the earth element."
The blood vessels constitute the water element;
warmth constitutes the fire element;
and the inhalation and exhalation of breath constitute the wind element.
If one opposes the earth element, there will be no body;
if one opposes the water element, the channels and rivers will become obstructed;
if one opposes the fire element, one will be unable to digest or assimilate.
When it is contrary to the wind element, the breath ceases; therefore,
compliance is taken as the essence of liberation,
while contrariety is taken as the continuity of bondage.
Conformity is the essence of liberation, while opposition is the continuity of bondage;
thus, opposition is called the root of illness.
The four hundred and four illnesses arise from such opposition.
"Immeasurable liberations arise from accord with Suchness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the thorough understanding of the essence of the four great elements is called the True Ultimate."
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have not yet received the instructions and entrustment of the Great Master;
we only pray that the Great Master, out of compassion and pity, will provide clear instruction to untie the bonds of sentient beings.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
"Form is identical to the four great elements;
I shall now further explain feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness for you all."
Experience occurs without discernment.
Because there is no discernment, one experiences gain and loss, right and wrong, identity and difference all at once.
This simultaneous experiencing is called "conformity."
To immediately accept liberation and yet falsely debate gain and loss, right and wrong, is called "successive bondage" and is also termed the "root of illness."
Perception (saṃjñā) perceives various objects— whether good or evil, gain or loss, fragrance or stench—
and apprehends them all without discrimination.
Because it does not discriminate, it is able to perceive universally.
Because conditions are like the unconditioned, it is called liberation.
To falsely engage in conceptual discrimination is termed the source of affliction.
When the practitioner moves through both the realms of right and wrong, as well as gain and loss, they do not turn their back on the non-existent nor cling to the existent.
Therefore, it is called liberation.
To deviate from suchness and follow [conceptual] names is termed the root of illness.
The cognizer universally takes the sense-gates as its object, making no distinction between the defiled and the pure.
To employ the faculties without discriminating between defilement and purity is called liberation;
if one violates even a single faculty, it becomes the source of illness.
Why is this? To accord with suchness without opposition is called "embodied understanding.
Embodied understanding is without bondage and flows according to its own nature.
Because it flows in accordance with its own nature, all bodily marks—the functions of greed, hatred, and delusion—are liberated.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as for what you call 'conformity'—"
In what sense is "conformity" (ānulomika) conformable to conformity?
Furthermore, it is said to "follow the natural flow" (svabhāva-pravṛtta); in what sense does it follow the natural flow?
Because they cannot comprehend the subtle and profound teachings of the Sage,
I only pray that you will instruct them so that they may take refuge, submit, and realize the truth.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
What you have asked is of great benefit.
I shall now explain it clearly for you.
Regarding your question as to what it is that accords with the "accordant" and thus accords with accord: [it is the path].
Because one accords with one's own nature by means of that very nature,
we know that accord with nature constitutes the noble,
while opposition to nature constitutes the ordinary.
To accord with nature by means of acceding to nature—
therein is neither acceding nor nature.
It is called "accoding" only in reference to what is contrary.
To go against [existence] is to perish with it;
to follow [the path] is to transcend it. This is liberation.
"Going against" refers to the succession of karma.
Following [this view] is called the bondage of karma;
once that which continues the bondage has perished,
liberation likewise does not exist.
It further states: "Regarding 'flowing according to its own nature,' what does it mean to flow according to its own nature?
Because it flows according to its own nature, it manifests as reflections throughout the gates of the sense organs and within the entire body."
By means of following, following, and following— following is all-pervasive;
because there is nothing it does not pervade, the nature follows and flows with the nature.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma,
from the summit of the world above down to the palaces of the six heavens of the desire realm, all shook and trembled.
An immeasurable great assembly, overcome by joy, unconsciously leaped up and threw themselves before the Buddha.
At that time, there was among the assembly a Great Being named Lingzhen (Vimala),
who, with the fierce and fearless power of a majestic roar, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Where will such a person as this— one who has realized the essence— be reborn?"
The Buddha told Lingzhen:
"One who realizes and understands in this manner is not encompassed by the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
Such a person shall be born within the transformed city of Maitreya Buddha’s realm in the city of Ketumatī."
With ears attuned to every sound, they appear and disappear following the Buddha.
Chapter Six: Revealing that All Sentient Beings Have the Buddha as Their Father and Mother within Their Own Bodies. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
The World-Honored One has realized and returned to the truth as described above.
All bodily forms are the functioning of liberation.
All sentient beings, from the level of the *pariccheda-śarīra* (segmented body) downward, possess bodily forms based on their reliance upon parents as causes and conditions.
Since the physical form has already manifested, it is termed the "body as the function of liberation.
If the physical forms of all sentient beings were entirely liberated,
this liberation would exist just as it does based on its causes and conditions, such as those derived from one's parents.
Therefore, one should know that the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha, the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha, and the Vipākakāya Buddha also have parents. Why is this so?
Because the Nirmāṇakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Vipākakāya Buddhas undergo birth.
Since all who are born must have parents, if the Buddha has parents,
I pray that you will speak of them.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
"As for what you said—that all sentient beings who seek the Way rely upon their parents as the cause for their growth, and this is called liberation."
Using such categories for comparison,
I shall now extensively explain and reveal them for you.
Although the true locus is one, the names established for it are immeasurable.
Although names are infinite, they all arise from the basis of karmic response.
Now, for the sake of opening up this response, they are named "Father" and "Mother. Why is this so?
Regarding the Buddha-parents within the bodies of all sentient beings:
the Supreme Reality of the Great Sun (Sūrya) is already the father,
and the Unobstructed Divine Nature is already the mother.
Quiescence and illumination together constitute the father;
illumination and quiescence together constitute the mother;
the primordial truth constitutes the father.
The zero-dwelling has already become the mother.
Thus, the parents give birth to that which corresponds to the Buddha, accords with the Buddha, and is the true recompense for the Buddha—a reality that is fundamentally nameless.
Yet, in order to guide those who have not yet awakened, it is designated by means of names.
When the arising of names is insufficient and their cessation remains,
the unimpeded Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have already declared that the True Ultimate of the Sun is the Father."
Non-obstruction as the divine nature has already become the mother;
stillness-illumination has already become the father;
illumination-stillness has already become the mother.
Heaven and Earth have already become my father and mother;
yet I have not received instruction regarding the origin of my birth.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
"The ultimate reality of the great sun is the profound origin of the fundamental goodness and evil of sentient beings."
The myriad consciousnesses disperse within the abode of the Dharma-realm in a state of chaotic stillness.
As they descend and flow downward, they are named the "Father.
Through non-pervasive resonance, reflections manifest in accordance with that response.
They are called mothers.
From these parents, one is born to accord with the Buddha, to respond to the Buddha, and to repay the Buddha;
one experiences the ultimate truth of the sun.
The manifestation of valorous spiritual powers and the non-abiding of the faculties extend through a thousand variations of illumination and function;
when these thousand variations of function are quiescent, this is the illumination of the Real.
When the inner radiance of the Real is bright, it is called the True Illumination.
True illumination illuminates the true; this interpenetration is great quiescence.
This quiescence is like constant awakening, which is called "arising in response.
This awakening is serene and empty, which is called "arising through conditions."
To be serene, empty, and all-encompassing is called the retribution of birth.
Retribution, conditions, responses, and so forth are all the functioning of quiescence.
When this functioning returns to quiescence, there is neither quiescence nor non-quiescence.
The substance dissolves and the characteristics merge, such that both identity and difference vanish.
If one wishes to say it exists, its form is not seen;
if one wishes to say it does not exist, the principle of emptiness issues forth as scripture.
Neither existent nor non-existent, the myriad phenomena arise therefrom.
Having heard the Dharma with joy, the unimpeded Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva praised it in verse:
"Vast and ever-unclouded, Luminous yet not clear."
The clear and the turbid merge or do not merge; Thus it is named "Birthless and Birthless" and the "Great One (Taiyi) Truly Without Seams.
Amorphous and chaotic, the flow of right and wrong has no distinct function; Each and every thing is not solitary or rigid.
Each one is infinite; The infinite within each one flows through the entire dharma-realm, Ever full yet never overflowing.
Each one universally contains; The universal containment resides within each one.
Within the circle, one returns to principle and transcends it; Without breath or form, the substance encompasses all, with neither interior nor exterior.
Since interior and exterior are encompassed within, right and wrong have no difference or sameness. The mind of faith is a clear, flowing river.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed:
"Listen attentively now;
I shall speak again in verse."

Their bodies are mutually accommodative and equal to space; they receive both the right and the wrong without self or other, loving what is right and turning away from what is wrong without derangement. Throughout kalpas they have increased their calamities and misfortunes;
at that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed heard the Dharma and rejoiced.
"May all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm together constantly hear the profound Dharma, realize its essence, and return to the truth.
Chapter Seven: Counteracting and Taking Medicine to Cure Disease. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, all sentient beings cherish their bodies and lives and give rise to immeasurable inversions;
though they hear the profound Dharma, they are unable to thoroughly and fundamentally comprehend its source.
It is, for example, as if there were a person for whom life itself is the very foundation.
Although life and spirit must depend upon food, drink, and clothing to remain sustained,
though I have received the World-Honored One’s instruction on the essential points of the profound and ultimate path of truth,
my body remains rigid, my mind like unrefined ore, my thoughts restless, and my heart flighty.
Unable to proceed upon the path to ascend into the true circle,
one takes the wondrous nature of the heavenly truth as the Dharma-body and must accord with the profound mystery to establish it as the life-force of wisdom.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the method for subduing the stubborn and unruly, so as to adorn the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
It is well that you now ask about this principle of mutual necessity.
It is like a person who has lived in poverty for a long time and, finding no means of relief,
reflects in silent contemplation.
"I am now poor and ill; unable to obtain gold for myself, I have no means to cure my ailment.
Gold that has an owner is difficult to acquire, but gold without an owner may be taken and used by me as I please."
Furthermore, it was heard that there is a mountain of gold in the world;
although the gold is immeasurable, it remains within the ore,
which is so hard and brittle that it cannot withstand hammering.
If one examines its mineral color, it is no different from gold;
yet although the ore is indeed gold, it is not fit for the use of gold. Why is this?
Because he has not yet been subdued and has not yet entered the furnace for smelting,
that poor man again thinks to himself:
I wish to seek out a dwelling to eliminate poverty and illness;
yet, lacking the necessary means, it cannot be achieved even with my own eyes.
To obtain gold, one must necessarily possess the tools for acquiring gold.
As for those who take up the tools for goldwork, they may obtain a furnace, charcoal, sweet and bitter ores, hammers, tongs, and the necessary labor, provisions, and stores;
yet, though they have these implements, they do not find a goldsmith.
Lacking skillful means, he still does not obtain the gold.
He then thinks further:
"Where might there be a skilled goldsmith?"
"I shall seek him out.
Then a voice from the sky spoke to him as if in speech:
"If you seek the Teacher with a mind so focused on gold that you exclude all greed, you will not find him."
"The place where I instruct you is located within the Palace of Purple Purity on Mount Taifu.
There, I engage in discussion together with various sages and worthies.
I have now fully instructed you regarding that place; do you not know how to seek this golden dharma? Can it be obtained?"
Upon hearing this, the poor man was filled with great joy;
he then proceeded on his knees, traveling directly for three hundred *li* until he reached his destination.
His two knees were so severely chafed that he did not even notice they had lost their kneecaps.
Thereupon, he knelt before his master and requested the method for extracting the gold.
With such single-minded devotion and reverence, he was unaware of the pain from his wound.
The goldsmith said to him:
"This Dharma is extremely profound and must not be treated lightly.
However, let us together observe that the Tathāgata’s intention lies in penetrating the core; having reached this limit, we shall never again be in disagreement.
You yourself must subdue your own pride."
He observed a hundred days of fasting and maintained strict seclusion.
Having established a solemn oath to revere [the teachings], he was granted [the transmission].
He then followed his teacher’s instructions and subdued his own pride.
He observed a hundred-day fast, dwelling in strict seclusion.
Having set a deadline and made a solemn vow, he went to the master’s residence.
The master, perceiving his intent, wept as he spoke to him, saying:
"If you encounter a worthy and virtuous person on the way, transmit it to them;
if you do not encounter such a worthy person, do not pass it on even to your own son.
Observing your single-minded devotion, I see that you have understood it upon hearing it in its entirety."
"Come, I shall bestow upon you the Dharma of true gold.
The Dharma of true gold does not exceed a mere inch of silk.
Take it with you and apply it accordingly."
The poor man, having obtained it, was filled with great joy.
The brave warrior returned home and had it fashioned according to the Dharma;
consequently, his wealth increased, and he personally relieved the poverty of himself, his wisdom, and his kinsmen.
To illustrate this by analogy:
the precious gold of the wisdom-life and Dharma-body exists within the impure ore of one's own self-reliance, coarse wool-like thoughts, and floating mental anxieties.
Unless it is subdued by oneself, there is no way for it to manifest.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I now behold this Great Sage as the supreme, true gold—the Dharma-body and life-force of wisdom that emerges from within the bodies of all sentient beings."
"Great Master, I only pray that you will instruct me on the method for bringing it forth.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed: "It is well said;
you have asked with great skill about the true gold of the Buddha-nature—the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom within the bodies of all sentient beings."
"I shall now expound for you the method and principles thereof.
At that time, there was among the assembly a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Samantagaurava, who,
filled with immeasurable joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for me the essential teaching for removing the dross from the true gold of the Buddha-nature within the bodies of all sentient beings, so that it may be fully purified and extracted.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pien-ching, saying:
All sentient beings abide in self-conceit;
their breasts are filled with notions of right and wrong, and they increase and decrease through the two views.
Arrogant and self-reliant, they delight in seeking victory and deceiving others.
They plunder and seize what they hold dear, leading their teachers and elders into perilous depths;
they treat their actual parents with contempt and inflict harm upon sentient beings at will.
They obscure the Buddha-nature, treating it like gold ore for the purpose of smelting.
You now inquire about the methods for bringing them forth;
I shall now point out to you the essential points regarding their classification and practical application. Why is this?
From the highest dragons and elephants down to the smallest insects and ants,
all sentient beings therein revere him as a Buddha;
they cherish all his sounds as if they were the Dharma.
One does not give rise to discrimination between good and evil, bearing them upon one's head as if they were the Saṅgha;
one regards even charcoal as something to be taken up,
and honors all sentient beings as if they were the Buddha.
Eliminate their pride and arrogance;
revere all sounds and cherish them as the Dharma.
Eliminate the two views of affirmation and negation, as well as increase and decrease.
They do not give rise to discrimination regarding good or evil, but revere them as they would the Sangha;

except for those who are competitive, deceitful toward others, or who seize what is beloved, ensnare their teachers and elders, or assault and strike their parents, and who inflict harm upon sentient beings with impunity.
By using these three medicines to eliminate the diseases of the three preceding poisons,
it is called "attaining charcoal.
One should always occupy the lowest of the low positions, advancing others while withdrawing oneself.
Having reflected on the removal of what has passed and not speaking of others' shortcomings,
one takes this as the fire of wisdom.
While this fire has not yet been extinguished, he spoke in verse:
High sources do not retain water; the most limpid waters are those into which all streams flow.
Subdue pride and learn humility; the stream of Dharma flows naturally.
Abide by this flow of Dharma, and it will always blaze forth; first, one must follow it downward.
Within the vessel of faith, tears pool; dwelling resolutely therein, one maintains death and sweeps away disputes.
When the household is settled and external conditions extinguished, those who harbor enmity are seen as one and the same, and the Dharmakāya shines forth in its perfect clarity.
Renouncing his body, he constantly dwelt in humble circumstances;
maintaining a mind of reverence, he served as a slave to provide for all beings, never ceasing until the very end.
Having paid universal homage to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, his mind was suddenly and completely liberated, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, all sentient beings who possess form and life vie for superiority rather than for inferiority;
they all vie for victory rather than for being swallowed up.
All [beings] contend at the beginning as if they would not contend at the end. Therefore,
from the highest reaches of the six desire realms down to the depths of the ocean of consciousness,

among all sentient beings therein, none are seen to harbor contention in their lower strata, nor to consume contention, nor to contend later, nor to contend with contempt, nor to contend with base motives, nor to contend through ignorance.
Therefore, the practitioner should always abide in non-contention;
then enmity and hatred will naturally cease, and calamities will have no cause to arise.
May you fulfill this vow by receiving and upholding these verses as they are spoken.
I discard what the multitude gathers; I gather what the multitude discards.
Left to wander at will, following the dust of the world, Without seeking pleasure, it comes to me of its own accord.
What the multitude discards, I alone preserve; What the multitude preserves, I abandon.

He does not contend with anyone out of attachment; free from contention, he wanders at ease and returns to the Dharma community, universally honoring Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. He addressed the Buddha as follows:
"World-Honored One, the glowing coals have already appeared."
"The rest remains incomplete;
I pray that out of great compassion you will graciously explain the full ordination once more.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantagupta, saying:
The simultaneous fusion of the myriad phenomena is called the cauldron;
their dissolution back into great quiescence is called the refining furnace.
The ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) responding to conditions serves as the bellows.
When struck by the hammer, it melts away, and the refined gold appears.
If a person can practice according to the Dharma in this way,
they will wash away the stubborn ore.
The radiance of the Dharma-body of the noble life shines brilliantly;
it is empty and unobstructed, all-pervasive and sovereign.
Furthermore, it is like a king of bees who leads his retinue into an empty tree to make it their dwelling.
The queen bee said to her offspring,
"You must exert diligent effort to produce honey.
Having received these instructions, the bees applied themselves with increased energy, and only then was the honey produced.
Once the honey has been produced, someone may encounter it and immediately think:
"Honey is the supreme flavor in the world; I shall certainly take it by means of skillful means."
To obtain honey, one must first approach the tree with a raft, remove the bees, and only then take the honey.
Once the honey has been obtained, one uses it respectfully for oneself and bestows its benefits upon one's kin.
In the same way, the Dharma-body of the life of wisdom resides within the tree of my own view.

They are arrogant, envious, and preoccupied with gain and loss, right and wrong, and empty talk; they exalt themselves while defiling others, and with pride and conceit, they insult and slander the virtuous and good, whom the swarms of bees protect.
First one must cut down the tree and then remove the bees;
only then can one attain the Buddha-nature of natural truth.
This wisdom-life and Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished, neither decays nor perishes.

The True Suchness is like honey; naturally reverent, it employs itself to accord with the mundane dust without being defiled, bestowing its benefits upon the immeasurable and teaching people the correct path.
By these causes and conditions, it serves as an antidote, like taking medicine.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pien-ching addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the raft-tree is felled by the axe;
the bee is driven away by the person."
I do not know by what method one obtains the raft that cuts down the tree of the view of self;

nor by what method one subdues the bees and insects of arrogance, malice, jealousy, gain and loss, right and wrong, idle chatter, self-exaltation, turbidity toward others, pride, insolence, and the slandering of the virtuous and noble.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, vowed to explain it fully for them.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed, saying:
"It is like dust that does not stain, being one with other things."
Therefore, it is called the "raft" and the "tree of self-view.
Upon awakening to their faults, one immediately reforms them; all signs vanish and worldly afflictions return to stillness.
Hence, it is said that the bees are removed.
When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable and limitless sentient beings rejoiced greatly, received it upon their heads, and practiced it accordingly.
Chapter Eight: Removing the Disease of Sentient Beings Cultivating the Path to Become Buddhas. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Unobstructed addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, throughout the past, present, and future, thousands of worthies and ten thousand sages have attained Buddhahood by practicing the path from the gradual to the sudden.
For what reason does the Tathāgata today preach that one must lose the Way, extinguish the mind, and cease thoughts, halting chapters and severing phrases?
When both the ordinary person and the Buddha are merged, the profound fruits are simultaneously lost;
there is no Buddha-fruit for the Buddha, and no entry into sainthood for the ordinary person.

Chapter Sixteen: On the Propagation. Furthermore, the Upāya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, what shall this sutra be named, and how should it be upheld?
We pray that the Bhagavān will explain this clearly,
so that all practitioners may receive the Buddha’s teachings."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Upāya, saying:
"This sutra is titled 'The Sutra on the Ultimate Great Compassion, Yearning, and Transformation.
It is also titled 'The Sutra on the Mutual Discussion of the Dharma between Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.'"
It is also called the *Secret Perfect Teaching Sūtra*;
it is also called the *Sūtra on the Non-transmigration of All Things*;
it is also called the *Sūtra on Transformation and Non-transformation*.
It is also titled *The Sutra on Ultimate Bodhi Without Arising or Non-arising*.
Those who wish to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra must cause both right and wrong to be simultaneously extinguished, merging gain and loss into a single unity.
That the myriad phenomena do not transmigrate is itself the Buddha-wisdom.
If one can act in this way, they are called a practitioner who upholds the sutra.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Upāya addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Upāya:
Its self-nature is primordially pure and perfect, a luminous illumination not produced by cultivation through external objects;
therefore, it is called "ultimate.
As for "great," nothing in the myriad things can contain it.
This is called "Great.
As for compassion, it is that which instructs all living beings;
this is named "compassion."
Those who possess compassion love sentient beings as they do their own marrow and eyes;
this is termed "compassion" (*anukampā*).
Therefore, it is called ultimate great compassion and compassion.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Upāya again addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Upāya: "To transform means to transform the ordinary person so they enter the state of sagehood;

To transform from darkness into light,
and to transform from birth-and-death into nirvana—
this is what is called "transformation."
"Transformation" refers to turning suffering into happiness and transforming diverse physical forms back into the principle of formlessness;
this is what is called "transformation."

As for a *sūtra*, from beginning to end, its sixteen chapters open up categories of meaning while the characters are joined together;

The names of the sūtras are numerous;

If there are practitioners who recite, uphold, and extensively explain this to others,
